claims.text: Strength and hardness in single-phase high-entropy alloys are primarily governed by edge-dislocation activity rather than screw-dislocation activity.
Nanoscale grain refinement produces a higher density of edge dislocations.
Grain boundaries associated with nanoscale refinement increase resistance to plastic flow.
Refining an HEA below a critical grain size produces inverse Hall–Petch softening.
The complex chemistry of HEAs increases lattice friction.
Increased lattice friction suppresses conventional screw-dislocation motion and favors edge-dislocation activity.
Decreasing grain size increases the density of grain boundaries, whose barrier effect raises hardness and yield strength up to a critical refinement level.
Below the critical grain size, deformation shifts to grain-boundary sliding or dynamic softening.
Intermediate-grain-size samples will have greater hardness and yield strength than the coarse-grained baseline because edge-dislocation motion is more effectively inhibited.
Further refinement beyond a critical grain size will reduce strength.
In a conventionally processed coarse-grained HEA, traditional dislocation mechanisms dominate and the edge-dislocation density is lower.
Edge dislocations can be prevalent and can control plasticity in at least one BCC alloy, contrary to the usual screw-dominated behavior of conventional BCC metals and many other HEAs.
Conventional thermally activated screw-dislocation theories do not explain the retained high-temperature strength plateau reported for NbTaTiZrV0.5.
The proposed behavior applies to compositionally homogeneous, single-phase FCC as well as BCC HEAs.
The proposed behavior should hold below the onset of diffusion-controlled softening, typically below 0.5–0.6 of the melting temperature.
Secondary phases, significant ordering, oxidation, or other environmental alteration may invalidate the proposed behavior.
The relative contributions of edge-dislocation mechanisms and grain-boundary sliding are not quantitatively determined and may depend on alloy chemistry and test conditions.
The critical grain size for the transition from Hall–Petch strengthening to softening is not specified and may vary with alloy chemistry and testing conditions.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis broadly states that edge-dislocation activity primarily governs single-phase HEAs, while the coarse-grained baseline is also an HEA but is said to be dominated by traditional dislocation mechanisms. The hypothesis does not clearly limit edge dominance to the refined state or explain the proposed transition with grain size.
